questions.question: Q: What is an anticline and how does it form?

points.text: An anticline is an arch-shaped upfold in rock layers. It forms when compressive forces at a convergent boundary buckle rock layers upward. The oldest rocks are exposed in the core of the anticline.

questions.question: Q: How do fold mountains differ from fault-block mountains?

points.text: Fold mountains form by compression, rock layers buckle into folds at convergent boundaries (e.g. Himalayas). Fault-block mountains form by tension, normal faults cause blocks to drop down, leaving adjacent blocks standing high (e.g. Sierra Nevada).

questions.question: Q: What is a nappe and where would you find one?

points.text: A nappe is a large-scale recumbent fold where rock layers have been overturned and thrust over younger rocks. They form under intense compression in major mountain belts like the Alps.

questions.question: Q: Name three major fold mountain ranges and state which plate collision caused each.

points.text: Himalayas (India colliding with Eurasia), Alps (Africa colliding with Eurasia), Andes (Nazca subducting under South America).

questions.question: Q: How does isostasy relate to mountain building?

points.text: When continental crust thickens during orogeny, the thickened crust floats higher on the mantle (like a thicker iceberg floats higher). This is isostatic uplift. Erosion later removes material, causing isostatic rebound as the crust rises further.
